key_terms.meaning: Linear or nonlinear system that maps the true image f(x,y) to an observed image before noise is added.
Random signal added to the degraded image: g(x,y)=H[f(x,y)]+n(x,y).
Noise whose amplitude has a normal probability density; it is reduced well by linear averaging.
Impulse noise that sets random pixels to black or white; it is reduced well by median filtering.
Spatial filter that replaces a pixel by the average of its neighbourhood, reducing Gaussian noise but blurring edges.
Order-statistic filter that replaces a pixel by the median of its neighbourhood, removing impulses with less edge blur.
Filter whose smoothing strength depends on local variance compared with noise variance.
Frequency-domain filter that sets selected narrow frequency bands to zero, used against periodic noise spikes.
Restoration filter that estimates F(u,v)=G(u,v)/H(u,v), unstable where H(u,v) is small.
Minimum mean square error filter that divides by |H|² plus a noise-to-signal term, limiting amplification where H is weak.
Set of line integrals of an image at many angles, forming projections used in tomography.
Reconstruction method that filters each projection with a ramp-like filter and back-projects it over the image plane.
Waste caused by using fixed-length code words for symbols that occur with unequal probabilities.
Waste caused by correlation between neighbouring pixels in an image.
Information that the human eye does not notice easily and can be discarded in lossy compression.
Entropy coder that builds an optimal prefix code by repeatedly merging the two least probable symbols.
Entropy coder that maps a whole symbol sequence to one interval or fraction instead of giving each symbol a separate code word.
Coding that replaces a run of repeated values by one value and a count.
Coding that stores the error between a pixel and a prediction from its neighbours.
Coding that transforms a block to concentrate energy in few coefficients, then quantizes and entropy-codes them.

takeaways: Image restoration starts from a model g(x,y)=H[f(x,y)]+n(x,y); without a model, filtering is only guesswork.
The probability density of noise decides which restoration filter is suitable.
Averaging reduces Gaussian noise but blurs edges; median filtering removes impulse noise while preserving edges better.
Adaptive filters change their strength according to local variance, so flat areas are smoothed more than detailed areas.
Periodic noise appears as spikes away from the spectrum centre and is removed by notch filtering those spikes.
Inverse filtering is unstable when H is small; the Wiener filter controls this by adding a noise-to-signal term.
The Radon transform collects line integrals, and filtered back-projection reconstructs an image by ramping projections before back-projecting them.
Compression works by finding and removing coding, interpixel and psychovisual redundancy.
Practical compression pipelines combine prediction or transform coding with quantization and an entropy coder such as Huffman, arithmetic or run-length coding.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress the full degradation model, noise-specific filters, periodic-noise notch filtering, inverse-versus-Wiener reasoning, Radon and filtered back-projection steps, and the compression chain from redundancy through entropy coding to predictive and transform coding.

bank.q: Explain the image degradation and restoration model g(x,y)=H[f(x,y)]+n(x,y). Define each term and list the steps used to restore an image.
outline: Define f, H, n and g.
Explain linear shift-invariant H and the point spread function.
State that restoration estimates H and noise statistics before applying an inverse operation.
Mention spatial and frequency-domain restoration paths.

bank.q: Describe common noise probability density models and explain which restoration filter suits each model.
outline: Gaussian noise and linear averaging.
Salt-and-pepper or impulse noise and median filtering.
Uniform, exponential or Rayleigh noise as examples of density-based models.
Relationship between noise shape and filter choice.

bank.q: Explain mean, order-statistic and adaptive filters for restoration when noise is the only degradation.
outline: Arithmetic mean, geometric mean and harmonic mean filters.
Median, max and min filters as order-statistic filters.
Adaptive local noise reduction using local mean and local variance.
Trade-off between noise removal and edge blur.

bank.q: Explain periodic noise reduction using frequency-domain filtering. Include the role of a notch filter.
outline: Periodic noise gives spike pairs away from the spectrum centre.
Notch filter zeroes selected frequency spikes.
Inverse transform gives the restored image.
Why this is cleaner than broad low-pass filtering.

bank.q: Define coding redundancy, interpixel redundancy and psychovisual redundancy. Explain how compression ratio and data redundancy are measured.
outline: Coding redundancy from unequal symbol probabilities.
Interpixel redundancy from correlation between neighbours.
Psychovisual redundancy from human visual limits.
Compression ratio and relative data redundancy formulas.

bank.q: A small grayscale image is corrupted by salt-and-pepper noise. Compare the result of a 3×3 arithmetic mean filter and a 3×3 median filter, and explain which is preferred.
outline: Mean filter spreads impulse values into neighbours.
Median filter rejects isolated black or white impulses.
Edge preservation is better with median filtering.
State the limitation of median filtering for heavy Gaussian noise.

bank.q: Given symbol probabilities, construct a Huffman code, draw the code tree, and compute the average code length and entropy.
outline: Merge two least probable symbols repeatedly.
Assign 0 and 1 to branches.
Read code words from root to leaf.
Compute average length and compare with entropy.

bank.q: Explain run-length encoding and decoding for a binary image, and show how Huffman decoding recovers a symbol stream from a code stream.
outline: Run-length pairs: value and count.
Encoding repeated runs in scan order.
Decoding by expanding counts.
Huffman decoding by walking the tree according to incoming bits.

bank.q: For a known degradation function H(u,v) and known noise-to-signal ratio, compare the frequency-domain forms of inverse filtering and Wiener filtering.
outline: Inverse filter F=G/H.
Amplification when H is near zero.
Wiener filter F=G H*/(|H|²+K).
Meaning of K as noise-to-signal term.

bank.q: Explain the Radon transform and describe the digital implementation of filtered back-projection for image reconstruction from projections.
outline: Line integrals at angle θ.
Sinogram formation.
Ramp or windowed ramp filtering of projections.
Back-projection and summation over angles.

bank.q: Analyze why inverse filtering amplifies noise. Derive or explain the Wiener filter and interpret each term in its frequency-domain expression.
outline: Small H causes large 1/H.
Noise is also divided by H.
Wiener filter uses H* and |H|² plus noise-to-signal term.
Limiting cases: no noise reduces to inverse filtering; large noise gives strong suppression.

bank.q: Compare predictive coding and transform coding. Design a block-based compression pipeline that includes quantization and entropy coding, and explain where loss occurs.
outline: Prediction from neighbouring pixels.
Transform such as DCT concentrates energy.
Quantization is the main lossy step.
Entropy coding of coefficients or prediction errors.
Trade-off between bit rate and visual quality.

bank.q: Evaluate Huffman coding, arithmetic coding and run-length coding for image compression. State when each is effective and where each is weak.
outline: Huffman is optimal prefix coding but needs integer code lengths and a code table.
Arithmetic coding approaches entropy more closely and handles skewed probabilities well.
Run-length coding works on repeated runs and is simple.
Choice depends on symbol statistics and image structure.

bank.q: A hospital needs low-dose CT reconstruction and long-term storage of images. Discuss suitable noise modelling, reconstruction filtering, and compression choices with their trade-offs.
outline: Noise model and noise level affect restoration and reconstruction.
Radon transform and filtered back-projection reconstruct CT slices.
Wiener or regularized restoration can reduce noise amplification.
Lossless coding for diagnosis; lossy coding for storage with quality limits.
Trade-offs among dose, noise, reconstruction speed, file size and diagnostic quality.

glossary.def: Process of estimating the true image from a degraded and noisy observed image using a degradation model.
Mathematical description of how an imaging system and noise transform the true image into the observed image.
Response of a linear imaging system to a point source, used as the spatial form of H.
Noise whose power is spread uniformly over all frequencies.
Noise that repeats at one or more frequencies and appears as spikes in the Fourier spectrum.
Filter that ranks neighbourhood pixel values and chooses one, such as the median or maximum.
Filter that replaces a pixel by an average of its neighbourhood values.
Filter whose behaviour changes with local image statistics such as mean and variance.
Frequency-domain filter that removes narrow selected frequency bands.
Restoration filter that divides the observed spectrum by the degradation function H.
Restoration filter that minimizes mean square error by balancing inverse filtering against noise amplification.
Transform that maps an image to its line integrals as a function of angle and offset.
Set of line integrals of an object along parallel lines at one angle.
Two-dimensional display of projections indexed by angle and offset.
Reconstruction step that smears each projection back across the image plane.
Ratio of the original data size to the compressed data size.
Average information per symbol in a source, measured in bits per symbol.
Code in which no code word is the beginning of another code word, allowing unique decoding.
Binary tree built by merging least probable symbols, used to assign Huffman code words.
Entropy coding method that represents a whole message by one number or interval.
Compression method that stores repeated values as a value-count pair.
Mapping of many possible values to a smaller set, usually the main lossy step in compression.
Orthogonal transform that concentrates energy of natural image blocks into few coefficients.
Compression method that codes the difference between a pixel and a prediction from nearby pixels.
Compression method that transforms blocks, quantizes coefficients, and entropy-codes the result.
